cells.tense: You're at a threshold right now and you can feel what's arriving without needing to force it. The ending already happened, or is happening, and you're not fighting it.
cells.ask: name one thing that's already ended and let it be ended — see what opens when you stop rehearsing it
cells.core: Something ended, and you didn't turn it into a war or a performance of moving on. You let it close, and because you let it close, what's arriving can actually reach you. That part is working — not because you're managing it, but because you're not.\n\nOut in the open, this looks like sitting at your own kitchen table and knowing which of the things on it are yours. You give what you can give and take what you're offered without keeping score in your head. That instinct is already fair. When something shows up now, meet it without pre-calculating whether you're getting your share — the balance holds itself when you don't squeeze it.
cells.sheetLine: You're letting the ending be an ending, and staying open to what comes next.
cells.verb: letting what's finished finish, so what's next can arrive
cells.place: at the threshold where what's outside enters your life now

cells.tense: You're bracing for a future you keep trying to force into shape. You can feel endings coming before they're here and you're reaching for them, clearing things out ahead of time. The clearing has become the habit.
cells.ask: let one thing you're about to end stay alive another day — feel where you actually are with it before you cut
cells.core: You're ending things before they've finished living. Something in you treats every loose end as a threat to be closed, so you close it early. But you're not free — you're just ahead of yourself, and the relief doesn't come.\n\nThe fear is real, but it's calling itself liberation. What's missing is the felt sense of connection — not to the thing you're cutting, but to yourself in the middle of it. That contact is what tells you when something's actually done versus when you're just scared. Let one thing stay open today. Not forever — just long enough to feel whether it's dead or you're running from it.
cells.sheetLine: You're closing doors that haven't closed yet, because you can't stand the waiting.
cells.verb: letting what's finished finish, so what's next can arrive
cells.place: at the threshold where what's outside enters your life now

cells.tense: You're still holding something that's finished, waiting at a threshold you already crossed. You've been calling it loyalty, or patience, or just not being ready yet.
cells.ask: pick one thing you've been keeping alive that's already gone — take one real step toward it being over, even just saying it out loud
cells.core: When this is flowing, you let things end on their own schedule. You can stand in a room where something just finished and feel the emptiness without filling it. And in that same room, you know instinctively what to give and what to keep — you don't treat the ending as a debt.\n\nThat's not where you are. You're protecting the shape of what used to be, and the holding is taking everything. It feels like faithfulness, but it's fear — fear that letting this go leaves you with nothing. One step, from feeling, from what actually moves you, is enough to start the current again. Not a leap. Just out of the doorway.
cells.sheetLine: You're calling it loyalty, but you're standing still at a threshold that's already behind you.
cells.verb: letting what's finished finish, so what's next can arrive

cells.tense: You're in the middle of something ending and you don't know it. You're still writing the next chapter as if nothing's changed. The clearing is happening around you, maybe through you, and you haven't claimed it as yours.
cells.ask: name one thing in your life that's already in the process of ending — say it plain, without making it a story
cells.core: When this is clear, you're the one who sees what's changing and says so. You organize around the truth of a situation, and people trust the steadiness in your voice. Things make sense when you're in the room because you're the one making them make sense.\n\nSomething in you is dying, or already dead, and you haven't noticed. Not because you're avoiding it — because it's happening without your name on it. You're arranging your days around a gap that's already here and calling it normal. The smallest act of ownership is just admitting what you already know. Then you can meet what's next with your eyes open.
cells.sheetLine: Something's already ending in you. You just haven't said it out loud yet.
